summary: Specifies the format for DHCPv4 client identifiers so they are interchangeable with the identifiers used in DHCPv6. It also corrects some problems in RFC 2131 and RFC 2132 in how client identifiers are handled. It is standards-track and updates RFC 2131, RFC 2132, and RFC 3315.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4361 gives DHCPv4 clients a stable identifier based on the same DUID used by DHCPv6. The identifier separates the host's identity from the identity of each network interface.

subtitle: A stable DHCPv4 client identifier that can be shared with DHCPv6.

tldr.problem: A DHCP client identified by its network interface address can appear to be a different client after hardware changes or when using multiple interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The client identifier option carries an IAID followed by a DHCP Unique Identifier, using the DUID format defined for DHCPv6.
tldr.outcome: A host can keep the same host identity across DHCP versions and network interfaces. RFC 4361 was later updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 4361 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2006. It was updated by RFC 5494 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: One Identity Across DHCP Versions
sections.content:
RFC 4361 specifies how DHCPv4 clients identify themselves. A conforming client places a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID), defined for DHCPv6, inside the DHCPv4 client identifier option.

The goal is for a device using both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 to present the same host identity. This can help services such as DNS updates that depend on the client's identity.
sections.plainLanguage: A device using both DHCP versions can present the same host identifier to each. The identifier does not depend on which version assigned its address.

sections.title: Problems with Hardware-Based Identity
sections.content:
The earlier DHCPv4 approach often used a network interface's link-layer address as the client identifier. Replacing the interface could change the client's identity and disconnect it from resources associated with the old identifier.

A host with wired and wireless interfaces could also appear as two clients. DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 used different identifier formats, so a dual-stack host could present different identities in each protocol. The older rules also allowed a client to omit the identifier option.
sections.plainLanguage: If an identifier comes from a network card, changing cards can change the client's identity. A computer with two cards can also look like two separate clients.

sections.title: Host Identity and Interface Identity
sections.content:
The identifier needs one part that remains unique to the host and another part that distinguishes the network identity being presented. RFC 3315's DUID and Identity Association Identifier (IAID) provide those parts.

The DUID identifies the host. The IAID distinguishes its network interfaces when needed. A client may use the same identifier on two interfaces when it wants them to receive the same address.
sections.plainLanguage: The DUID identifies the host, and the IAID can identify one of its network interfaces. This lets the host keep one identity while distinguishing its connections.

sections.title: The Client Identifier Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 client identifier option uses option code 61. To carry an RFC 3315-style binding identifier, the type field is 255, followed by the 32-bit IAID and then the DUID in the remaining option data.

The client sends this option in DHCPv4 messages. A client with stable storage MUST keep a generated DUID for later messages, including after an operating-system reboot.
sections.plainLanguage: The option contains a type value, a 32-bit interface identifier and the host's DUID. The DUID stays the same when the client restarts.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A conforming DHCPv4 client MUST send a client identifier containing an IAID and DUID. It MUST NOT identify itself only by a hard-wired layer-two address, except as allowed by RFC 3315. A dual-stack device SHOULD use the same DUID for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6, and a multi-interface client SHOULD use one DUID with a different IAID per interface.

A conforming DHCPv4 server MUST use the client identifier option when a client sends one. Servers that follow the older DHCP specifications do not need changes. Servers must still use the hardware fields to support older clients that send no identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: New clients always send the stable identifier. Servers use it when present and continue supporting older clients that omit it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no new security issues. It points to the existing DHCPv4 security discussion in RFC 2131 and DHCP authentication in RFC 3118, as well as the security discussion in RFC 3315 for DHCPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: This identifier format does not add new security protections or risks. Existing DHCP security guidance still applies.
